overview.text: A longitudinal wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium while the medium’s particles oscillate parallel to the wave’s direction of travel. The particles move back and forth around their usual positions; the traveling pattern, rather than the particles themselves, carries energy onward. This motion creates alternating compressions, where particles are crowded together and pressure is higher, and rarefactions, where particles are farther apart and pressure is lower. Longitudinal waves are also called compression waves. Familiar examples include sound traveling through air and seismic P waves traveling through Earth. Their defining feature—particle motion along the direction of travel—distinguishes them from transverse waves.

key_facts.text: “Compression wave” is another name for a longitudinal wave.
In a sound wave, compressions are higher-pressure regions and rarefactions are lower-pressure regions.
The wave pattern travels onward even though the medium’s particles oscillate around their equilibrium positions rather than traveling with the pattern.
Sound waves in air and most fluids are longitudinal; sound in solids can have both longitudinal and transverse forms.
Earthquake P waves are longitudinal: they compress and expand the ground in the direction the wave travels.
